subsection: 2. The marketing mix and the target market

notes.b: A business cannot control what customers think, but it can control a set of decisions about what it offers and how it offers it. That set of decisions is the marketing mix, and its aim is to satisfy the target market (the group of customers the business has chosen to serve).
points: The seven Ps in this course are product or service, pricing, promotion, people, packaging, process and place. Physical evidence is not one of them.
The target market shapes every element, because what customers want, can afford and respond to determines each decision. For example, a market of students suggests low prices and online promotion.
The mix matters because it determines whether customers buy, how much they pay and whether the business earns a profit. A good product with a poor price or the wrong outlet can still fail.

The Ps are interdependent: a premium price, for example, affects the packaging, the promotion and the choice of outlets. Inconsistency between them weakens the brand, because customers receive mixed signals.
notes.tip: When asked to outline the marketing mix, give all seven Ps from the list above, each with one decision applied to the business in the question. A common mistake is listing only four or five Ps, or adding physical evidence.

notes.b: The product or service is the core of the offer, so decisions about it come first. They cover its features, its quality, its brand and the range the business sells.
points: Features and quality set what the product does and how well it does it. They are judged against what the target market values, so a feature that matters to one market may be wasted on another.
Branding gives the product a name, identity and reputation that help customers recognise and trust it. This is a product decision, separate from the packaging that the product comes in.
The range offered (how many versions or sizes are sold) is part of the product decision, and it depends on the variety the target market expects.

The product life cycle (assumed knowledge: the stages a product passes through) runs through introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Each stage needs different marketing decisions, so the mix is not fixed.
A good is tangible (you can touch it), whereas a service is intangible. Services are usually described as intangible, variable and perishable, so their quality depends on the people delivering them.
notes.tip: Do not confuse branding with packaging. Branding is a product decision (name, identity, reputation); packaging is its own P covering protection, design and labelling.

notes.b: Pricing sets the amount customers pay. The price must cover costs for the business to make a profit, but the strategy chosen must also reflect competitors and what the target market will pay.
points: Cost-plus pricing adds a fixed mark-up to the cost of making or buying the product. It is simple, but it ignores what customers will actually pay.
Penetration pricing sets a low initial price to win market share quickly. It is often used for a new product in a competitive market, such as a sample budget cleaning product.
Skimming pricing sets a high initial price to reach customers who will pay more, then lowers it as competition grows. This is the opposite order to penetration, which starts low.
Competitive pricing sets prices in line with, or just below, rivals' prices, so the product is not seen as dearer than the alternatives.
Premium pricing sets a permanently higher price to signal quality or exclusivity, as a sample premium chocolate maker might. Unlike skimming, the price is not lowered later.
Psychological pricing uses figures such as 9.99 euro, which can make a price appear lower than a round figure would.

Loss leader pricing sells one product below cost to attract customers who are expected to buy other, more profitable products. It is a legitimate strategy, but the business accepts a short-term loss on the product.

The target market influences price through its income, its price sensitivity (how far demand falls when the price rises) and what it associates with quality. Fair pricing also means not exploiting vulnerable customers.
notes.tip: Common mistakes are confusing penetration with competitive pricing, and skimming with premium. Penetration starts low to win share; competitive matches rivals; skimming starts high then falls; premium stays high. For a discuss or evaluate question, weigh two strategies against the target market and end with a justified choice.

notes.b: Promotion communicates the offer to the target market and persuades customers to buy. A business usually combines several methods, known as the promotional mix, and chooses media where its customers spend their time.
points: Advertising is paid, non-personal communication (the same message goes to many people) through media such as television, radio, outdoor posters and online display.
Sales promotion uses short-term incentives such as discounts, coupons and competitions to encourage an immediate purchase.
Personal selling is one-to-one communication by a sales representative, which suits complex or high-value products because the customer's questions can be answered directly.
Public relations builds goodwill through media coverage, press releases and events. It is not paid for in the same way as advertising, which is why it is described as earned goodwill.
Sponsorship links a brand with an event, team or cause, so the brand's image benefits from the association.

Social media and influencer marketing create two-way engagement, because customers can reply and share. Influencers are paid to promote products to their own audiences, and paid or gifted posts must be labelled, for example #Ad, under CCPC and ASAI guidance from October 2023.
The target market decides the choice of media. A younger market reached mainly online suits social media, while an older, price-sensitive market may suit printed promotion.
Promotion should be honest and responsible, especially when aimed at children, because misleading claims harm customers and the brand's reputation.
notes.tip: Do not mix up advertising (paid, non-personal), sales promotion (short-term incentive), public relations (earned goodwill) and sponsorship (brand linked to an event). A common mistake is calling a discount advertising.

notes.b: People are the staff and others who deliver the product or service. Their skills, attitudes and behaviour shape the customer experience, so they are part of the mix and not just a cost.
points: Recruitment and training ensure staff have the skills and knowledge to meet the expectations of the target market.
In service businesses the employee is often the part of the offer the customer experiences most directly, so attitude matters greatly.
Motivation and reward systems keep staff focused on service quality and reduce staff turnover, which also saves the cost of recruiting replacements.
Customer-facing staff should suit the target market, such as knowledgeable advisers for a premium brand.
notes.tip: People means the staff delivering the offer, not the customers. Keep them separate from the target market in your answer.

notes.b: Packaging is more than a box. It protects the product and then communicates with customers through its design, materials and labelling.
points: Functional packaging protects the product in storage and transport, and it makes the product easier for the customer to handle.
Design and colour create brand recognition and attract attention at the point of sale (the place where the customer chooses and buys).
Labelling must give accurate information, such as ingredients, weight and use-by date, as required by law for many products. Honest labelling is also an ethical duty to customers.

Sustainable packaging, such as recyclable materials or reduced material use, can appeal to environmentally conscious customers. Packaging has environmental costs, and customers increasingly expect it to be recyclable.
The EU packaging and packaging waste regulation, Regulation (EU) 2025/40, applies from 12 August 2026, which shows why sustainable packaging matters to businesses.
notes.tip: Packaging is the P covering protection, design and labelling. Keep it distinct from branding, which is a product decision.

notes.b: Process is the system by which the product or service is made and delivered. It covers the steps, the speed and the ease of each stage for the customer.
points: Process decisions cover how orders are taken, how products are made or services delivered and how long each stage takes.
A simple, efficient process reduces waiting times and costs and improves the customer's experience.
Online ordering, self-service checkouts and tracked delivery are process choices that suit busy target markets. Digital tools like these change how the offer is ordered and delivered.
A process must be consistent, so that customers receive the same quality each time they buy.
notes.tip: Process is how the offer is delivered; place is where and through whom it is sold. A common mistake is treating them as the same thing.

notes.b: Place covers how the product reaches customers. The route it takes is called a channel of distribution, and the route may be direct or indirect.
points: A direct channel sells from producer to customer, such as a sample farm shop or the business's own website.
An indirect channel uses intermediaries (businesses between producer and customer) such as wholesalers and retailers, for example a sample manufacturer selling through supermarkets.
Online channels allow sale and delivery without physical outlets, widening reach but adding delivery costs. Delivery also has an environmental cost.
Location decisions for a physical outlet depend on where the target market shops, travels and works, so that customers can reach it easily.
notes.tip: Remember that a direct channel includes online selling by the producer. For a discuss or evaluate question on direct against indirect channels, weigh both sides for the stated business and give a justified choice.

keyTerms.definition: The set of controllable decisions a business makes about its offer, price, promotion and distribution to meet target market needs.
The stages a product passes through, from introduction to growth, maturity and decline.
A pricing method that adds a fixed mark-up to the cost of making or buying a product.
Setting a low initial price to win market share quickly, usually for a new product.
Setting a high initial price to attract customers willing to pay more, then lowering it as competition grows.
A product sold below cost to attract customers who are expected to buy other, more profitable products.
Pricing designed to influence how customers perceive a price, such as ending it in .99 or .95.
Short-term incentives such as discounts, coupons and competitions that encourage customers to buy now.
The route a product takes from producer to end customer, which may include wholesalers and retailers.
Partnering with people who have an online audience so they promote a product to their followers.

factCards.definition: Product or service, pricing, promotion, people, packaging, process and place.

questions.prompt: Explain the marketing mix for a business of your choice, showing how the target market shapes at least three of the seven Ps.
questions.model: Take a business selling premium craft chocolate to office workers in Dublin. The target market values quality and wants a treat at a convenient price. Product: the range focuses on small bars with distinctive flavours and clear sourcing, because the target market rewards quality. Pricing: a premium price is set above supermarket chocolate, with a small gift box at a higher price to reflect the brand. Promotion: the business uses social media and sampling at office lunchtime events, since office workers are reached through these channels. Packaging: the bars come in recyclable paper wrapping that suits a gift-buying market. Place: the business sells through delicatessens and a website with weekday delivery to offices, matching where the target market shops and works. Each P supports the others, so the premium price is consistent with the packaging, the promotion and the choice of outlets.

questions.prompt: Explain how a premium target market would influence the pricing strategy, promotion and place of a business, and identify the link between them.
questions.model: A premium target market is willing to pay more for quality and exclusivity, so the business would use premium pricing, setting its price above competitors to signal high quality. Promotion would be designed to reinforce that image, with high-quality advertising in lifestyle media, personal selling for corporate gifts and sponsorship of arts events that the target market attends. Place would be chosen to match the image, so the product would be sold through upmarket retailers and a carefully presented website rather than discount outlets. The link is consistency: a premium price loses credibility if promotion uses discounts or the product is sold in cheap outlets, so all three elements must send the same message.
